prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

While that my soul repairs to her devotion, Here I intomb my flesh, that it betimes May take acquaintance of this heap of dust; To which the blast of death's incessant motion, Fed with the exhalation of our crimes, Drives all at last. Therefore I gladly trustMy body to this school, that it may learn To spell his elements, and find his birth Written in dusty heraldry and lines ; Which dissolution sure doth best discern, Comparing dust with dust, and earth with earth. These laugh at jet, and marble put for signs,To sever the good fellowship of dust, And spoil the meeting. What shall point out them, When they shall bow, and kneel, and fall down flat To kiss those heaps, which now they have in trust? Dear flesh, while I do pray, learn here thy stem And true descent: that when thou shalt grow fat,And wanton in thy cravings, thou mayst know, That flesh is but the glass, which holds the dust That measures all our time; which also shall Be crumbled into dust. Mark, here below, How tame these ashes are, how free from lust, That thou mayst fit thyself against thy fall.

***

### The Academy of Dust: A Meditation on Mortality

To cultivate a life of true spiritual depth, a person must divide the labors of the self. While the soul ascends toward the divine through prayer, contemplation, and holy devotion, the physical body must be assigned a different task: to sit in solemn quiet and contemplate its own inevitable end. By committing the flesh to meditate upon mortality, the spirit is liberated to pursue the eternal, unburdened by the body's false pretensions of permanence.

In this spiritual discipline, the grave serves as a vital schoolhouse for the living flesh. It is within the stillness of the sepulcher that the physical self confronts its truest and most fundamental lesson—its lowly origin. Stripped of vanity and worldly pretense, the body learns that, regardless of health, beauty, or strength, it is fashioned from nothing more than humble dust, bound by an unyielding law to return to the earth from which it was formed.

Human pride often seeks to resist this truth through the erection of ornate funeral monuments, marble effigies, and elaborate tombs. Yet these grand structures fail to preserve human distinctions beyond the veil of life. Before the absolute reality of mortality, all social hierarchies crumble. Death functions as the ultimate equalizer, reducing the monarch and the laborer alike to identical, indistinguishable ash. In the quiet darkness beneath the stone, no monument can maintain the illusion of earthly superiority.

Confronted with this reality, the living body is revealed to be much like a fragile hourglass—a delicate, temporary vessel holding the very dust into which it will soon dissolve. Every passing moment is a grain of sand falling through the glass. Viewing the physical self through this metaphor serves as a powerful moral compass, providing a solemn reminder to restrain sinful ambitions and curb appetite for worldly cravings. When one recognizes how easily the glass can break, the desperate pursuit of fleeting pleasures loses its hold.

Ultimately, there is profound wisdom to be gained by observing the peaceful, desire-free state of those who have already returned to the earth. The buried ashes of the dead suffer no anxieties, harbor no greed, and feel no pain; they exist in absolute stillness. By reflecting on this tranquil end, the living body learns to shed its restless desires and quiet its fears, gradually preparing itself to meet its own inevitable death not with terror, but with serene acceptance.

***

### The Academy of Dust

How brief and treacherous is the tenure of human life, yet how fiercely we are tormented by the corrupting cravings of the flesh. We chase the fleeting shadows of earthly pleasure, building castles out of breath and appetite, even as time silently undermines the very ground upon which we stand. The body clamors for gratification, blinding the spirit to its own inevitable end. Recognizing this tragedy—that we spend our few, fragile years enslaved to passions that will perish with us—I chose to enact a symbolic death before my true one arrived. I resolved to withdraw from the clamorous world and deliberately entomb my living self within a quiet "school" of dust.

In this gloomy sanctuary of quietude, my curriculum is mortality itself. Surrounded by the cold stone of ancient tombs and the damp scent of charnel earth, I become a scholar of decay. I spend my hours deciphering the lesson plan written upon crumbling epitaphs and moss-eaten monuments. I observe how the grandest names of history are eroded by rain, and how the proudest forms of men are reduced to grey, anonymous earth. In watching the slow, relentless breakdown of bone and marble, I begin to understand the true texture of my own physical existence. Decay is not a tragedy to be mourned, but a teacher to be heeded.

Through this rigorous contemplation, a profound revelation takes hold: the human body is neither a fortress nor a temple of permanent delight, but merely a fragile hourglass crafted from clay. With every heartbeat, the grains of sand trickle down; with every breath, the vessel grows thinner. The flesh that once burned with feverish ambitions and insatiable lusts is destined to crumble into cool, lust-free ashes. Dust cannot hunger; ash cannot covet; the grave feels no burning temptation. The very desires that once threatened to consume my soul are revealed to be nothing more than smoke, bound to dissipate the moment the glass runs dry.

This realization works a quiet miracle upon the heart. By meditating on my eventual end, the wild, chaotic cravings of the flesh are finally tamed. Earthly desires lose their hypnotic power when held against the vast backdrop of eternity. I no longer view death with terror, but as a necessary purification—a return to stillness. By dying to the world in this humble school of dust, I have unburdened my spirit of its heaviest chains, standing at last fully prepared, purified, and at peace for the day my own hourglass finally runs clear.

Here I entomb my flesh, that it betimes

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 17th-century metaphysical poem about mortality, addressing one's own flesh and reflecting on how marble tombs fail to prevent our ultimate return to dust.
counterfactuals.output:
**TO MY FRAIL FLESH, UPON THE VANITY OF TOMBS**

Thou subtle weave of bone and scarlet thread,
Thou house wherein my soul is tenanted,
Frail Flesh, why art thou troubled thus to know
How soon thy fleeting canopy must go?
Thou art but Borrowed Earth, a painted shell,
Whose ruin every ticking pulse doth tell.

Yet Pride would dress thy ruin in Parian stone,
And build a palace for a bag of bone;
Gilded with epitaphs, proud men intend
To strike a marble truce with their own end:
As if a carved and solemn monument
Could cheat the worm, or break the element.

O fond Conceit! The cold, ambitious vault
Is but a static, glittering assault
On Truth itself. For Marble too is Dust—
A harder earth that yields to Time’s slow rust.
What boots it if the sculptured angels weep,
When under alabaster, ashen sleep
Dissolves the king as swiftly as the knave,
And makes the vault a pompous, dry-land grave?

The stone shall crumble as the marrow rots;
Time dulls the chisel, and the sentence blots.
Then sigh no more, my Flesh, for vaulted state,
Nor bribe the quarry to delay thy fate.
Let cold stone crack; the Maker knows the place
Where dust resides, till resurrected Grace
Shall strip this mortal cloak, and set us free
From marble's lie, and earth's captivity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem in the style of John Donne or George Herbert that uses extended metaphors of ashes, dust, and time to explore the decay of the physical body.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Holy Hour-Glass; or, The Sovereign Dust**

Look in this glass: I am that brittle frame
   Wherein the sands of stolen minutes run;
   My head the upper globe, which once begun
To drain its golden youth, now owns no name
   Save *ruin*. Every pulse-beat shakes the waist,
   And down to darkness are my remnants chased.

My bones were timber for a fevered fire,
   A hearth where youth’s bright embers leapt on high;
   Now cold white soot offends the watcher’s eye,
And grey ash chokes the furnace of desire.
   Time is the blowing wind that fans away
   The fleeting cinders of this ruin’d clay.

Ah, what is man but dust that walks a span,
   A walking sepulchre of his own decay?
   The worms wait hungry for their borrowed day,
To harvest all that proud ambition began.
   My sinews slacken, and my eyes grow dim,
   As slow oblivion steals from limb to limb.

Yet, sovereign Potter, whose almighty hand
   Did knead this breath into a handful dry,
   Shall Time’s swift hourglass leave me thus to die,
Unremembered in the drift of barren sand?
   No: Time is but Thy sieve, which shakes the chaff,
   To clear the earth, and print Thy holy graft.

Then break the glass, Lord! Let the ashes fall,
   And let this dust be scattered to the wind;
   For in the deep earth Thou shalt my atoms find,
And from these cinders build a heavenly hall.
   Death burns the house, but spares the founder’s mould,
   That from these ashes I may rise as gold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a classic devotional poem centered on death and the vanity of earthly monuments.
counterfactuals.output:
Here is an original devotional poem written in the classic 17th-century style (reminiscent of George Herbert and James Shirley), reflecting on the levelling power of death, the futility of grand tombs, and the true refuge of the soul.

***

### The Unlasting Stone

Go, carve thy name in polished brass,  
Or raise a vault of marble tall;  
Yet like the shadow on the grass,  
The proudest monument shall fall.  
The greedy worm heeds not the crown,  
Nor does the moss respect the spire;  
Time lays the golden sceptre down,  
And quenches every mortal fire.

The sculpted grief, the gilded phrase,  
Are swallowed in the silent dust;  
The boastful tombs of ancient days  
Are broken by the iron rust.  
For who can bind the fleeting breath,  
Or bribe the watcher at the grave?  
The high and low yield unto Death—  
The monarch slumbers with the slave.

O foolish man, to build thy peace  
Upon a piece of crumbling stone!  
When mortal pulse and labor cease,  
Thou standest at the throne alone.  
No marble cloak can hide the soul,  
No epitaph can plead thy cause,  
When life's brief book has closed its scroll  
Before the Lord’s righteous laws.

Lord, grave Thy name upon my heart,  
A monument of grace divine;  
That when this dusty frame shall part,  
My spirit may be truly Thine.  
Build me no tomb beneath the skies,  
Where pride and pale oblivion meet;  
Fit me to see Thy morning rise,  
And lay my crown before Thy feet. 

***

### Classic Historical Parallel
If you are also looking for a famous historical poem from the literary canon on this exact theme, consider **"Death the Leveller"** by James Shirley (1659):

> *The glories of our blood and state*  
> *Are shadows, not substantial things;*  
> *There is no armour against Fate;*  
> *Death lays his icy hand on kings:*  
> *Sceptre and Crown*  
> *Must tumble down,*  
> *And in the dust be equal made*  
> *With the poor crooked scythe and spade.*

counterfactuals.output:
Before this sepulchre of weathered stone,
I kneel in shadows where the ivy creeps,
And lift a whisper to the calm unknown,
Beside the vault where silent memory sleeps.

Listen, my flesh, that throbs with fleeting heat,
Hush the vain thunder of your restless veins;
Look down to where the quiet dark is sweet,
And see how little of our pride remains.

Oh body, learn humility from dust,
From these fine ashes sifted in the shade,
That once knew vigor, appetite, and trust,
Yet bowed to loam from which all things were made.

Unclench your fingers; lay your crowns aside.
The cold gray marble yields no room for state.
Death is the quiet leveller of pride,
Where small and sovereign share a common fate.

Lord, shape my posture while I yet draw breath;
Teach my warm clay the wisdom of the grave,
That long before I yield my form to death,
I live in meekness for the soul You saved.
